questions.q: What type of image (real/virtual, erect/inverted, magnified/diminished) is formed by a concave mirror when the object is placed between the pole and the focus?
questions.a: Virtual, erect, and magnified. A wrong answer (e.g., saying real or inverted) reveals the student has not linked the object position to the image characteristics taught in ray diagrams (c8_physics_ch6_5) and is likely memorising uses without understanding the underlying optics.

questions.q: Why does a dentist use a concave mirror instead of a plane mirror to examine a tooth?
questions.a: A concave mirror held close to the tooth (object between pole and focus) produces a magnified, erect, virtual image, allowing the dentist to see a larger view of the tooth. A plane mirror would give a same-size image. If a student says "concave mirrors always magnify", they are overgeneralising — they must specify the object must be within the focal length.

questions.q: In a car headlight, the bulb is placed at the focus of the concave reflector. If the bulb is accidentally shifted 2 cm away from the focus towards the mirror, what happens to the reflected beam and why?
questions.a: The reflected beam will diverge (spread out) instead of being parallel. When the source is between focus and pole, rays reflect as if coming from a virtual focus behind the mirror, producing a divergent beam. A wrong answer (e.g., "beam becomes more parallel") shows the student does not understand the reversibility of light paths: rays from focus go parallel; rays from inside focus diverge.

questions.q: Compare the object positions relative to the focal point for a shaving mirror and a headlight reflector. Explain why the shaving mirror must be held close to the face while the headlight bulb is fixed at the focus.
questions.a: Shaving mirror: object (face) is between pole and focus (u < f) → magnified virtual image. Headlight: source (bulb) is exactly at focus (u = f) → parallel beam. A student who says both are at the focus confuses the two distinct requirements: magnification needs u < f; collimation needs u = f.

questions.q: A student claims: "A concave mirror used as a shaving mirror forms a real image on the face." Evaluate this statement and correct the misconception.
questions.a: The statement is false. A shaving mirror forms a *virtual* image behind the mirror that appears magnified and erect. The image cannot be projected on a screen (the face). If the student thinks it's real, they confuse the magnified virtual image (u < f) with the magnified real image formed when the object is between focus and centre of curvature (f < u < 2f).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a concave mirror (e.g., a shiny steel spoon or a makeup mirror) to demonstrate all three uses: shaving, dentist, and headlight. List the steps and what you would observe in each case.
questions.a: A good answer includes: (1) Hold spoon close to eye → magnified erect image (shaving/dentist). (2) Hold spoon at arm's length → inverted diminished image (not a use). (3) Place a small LED bulb at the focal point of a larger concave mirror (or approximate with spoon and torch) → reflected beam becomes a narrow parallel patch on a distant wall (headlight). A poor answer misses the focal point demonstration or cannot explain why the bulb must be at the focus.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Concave mirrors are ______ mirrors that produce magnified, erect, virtual images when the object is placed between the pole and focus, and form real, inverted images when the object is beyond the focus; these distinct image properties are exploited in shaving mirrors (magnified virtual image), dentist mirrors (magnified virtual image), and headlight reflectors (parallel beam from source at focus).
Fill in the blank: Begin by asking students to ______ a steel spoon: the inner curved surface acts as a concave mirror.
What is Concave mirrors? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Concave mirrors are converging mirrors that produce magnified, erect, virtual images when the object is placed between the pole and focus, and form real, inverted images when the object is beyond the focus; these distinct image properties are exploited in shaving mirrors (magnified virtual image), dentist mirrors (magnified virtual.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Concave mirrors?
questions.a: Students often believe a concave mirror *always* produces a magnified image.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain, using ray diagram reasoning, why a concave mirror must be held close to the face for shaving, why a dentist places the mirror very near the tooth, and why a headlight bulb is positioned exactly at the focal point of the reflector.
